design_detail: Phase 3, randomized (1:1, stratified by site), double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial (MAPP1; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03537014) at 15 sites (11 in the United States, 2 in Canada, 2 in Israel; institutional sites and private clinics), recruiting from 7 November 2018 to 26 May 2020 (last visit 21 August 2020). After three 90-minute preparatory sessions and withdrawal of psychiatric medicines, 90 adults with severe PTSD (CAPS-5 total severity of 35 or more) were randomized to manualized therapy with MDMA or with an inactive placebo in three 8-hour experimental sessions about 4 weeks apart, each followed by three 90-minute integration sessions, with the same two-person therapist team. Primary end point: change in CAPS-5 total severity from baseline to 18 weeks (about 8 weeks after the third experimental session), rated by blinded independent raters over live video; key secondary end point: Sheehan Disability Scale (SDS). Sponsored and fully funded by the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS); designed, monitored and analysed by its wholly owned MAPS Public Benefit Corporation (MAPS PBC); protocol and statistical analysis plan developed with the FDA.
can_establish: Whether, in adults with severe, chronic PTSD who had stopped their psychiatric medicines, adding MDMA to three sessions of an intensive manualized therapy lowered clinician-rated PTSD symptoms at 18 weeks more than adding an inactive placebo to the same therapy, and which adverse events were more frequent with MDMA during the treatment period.
cannot_establish: Whether the difference comes from MDMA's pharmacology rather than from participants knowing or guessing their group (an inactive placebo was used and blinding was not formally assessed); whether the benefit lasts beyond about 2 months after the last session (no follow-up is reported); how MDMA-assisted therapy compares with trauma-focused psychotherapies or SSRIs (no such arm); rare or delayed harms, including later non-medical use (90 people over 18 weeks, with expected drug effects not solicited as adverse events); or effects in people the trial excluded (current alcohol or substance use disorders, personality disorders, uncontrolled hypertension or arrhythmia; the registry's current text, added in 2024, also excludes more than limited past ecstasy use).

sample.recruitment: Print and internet advertisements, referrals from treatment providers and word of mouth; participants had to contact the sites themselves, even if recommended by a provider. 1,331 people were phone-screened (986 excluded, 797 as unlikely to meet the criteria), 345 screened, 131 enrolled and 91 randomized (77 in the United States, 9 in Canada, 5 in Israel); 40 enrolled people were excluded before randomization, 20 for not meeting the criteria (Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph; Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1b).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: DSM-5 current PTSD for at least 6 months (MINI) and a CAPS-5 total severity of 35 or more at baseline, measured after any psychiatric medicine had been tapered for at least five half-lives plus 1 week (taper 0 to 103 days). Excluded: primary psychotic disorder, bipolar I disorder, dissociative identity disorder, eating disorders with active purging, major depression with psychotic features, personality disorders, current alcohol and substance use disorders, pregnancy or lactation, and medical conditions that would make a sympathomimetic drug harmful (uncontrolled hypertension, history of arrhythmia, marked QT prolongation); mild stable conditions such as well-controlled hypertension were allowed case by case (Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph; Procedures, 1st paragraph). The registry adds willingness to stay overnight after each session (in the record since registration); its current text also excludes people who had used ecstasy more than 10 times in the past 10 years or at all in the 6 months before the first session, or who had been in a MAPS MDMA trial, but that exclusion entered the record only on 28 October 2024 (version 57), after the trial: the versions current during the trial excluded only current illegal drug use, and the protocol (not read) may have contained it (registry record, Eligibility; History of Changes). Three protocol amendments during enrollment clarified comorbid medical conditions, added suicidal ideation and behaviour as adverse events of special interest and increased suicidality assessments after sessions (the last two at the FDA's request), and allowed some telemedicine visits (Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Mean age 41.0 (SD 11.9); 59 (65.6%) female at birth (two of them non-binary); 69 (76.7%) White and 8 (8.9%) Hispanic or Latino; mean duration of PTSD 14.1 years; dissociative subtype 19 (21.1%); comorbid major depression 82 (91.1%); 16 veterans (17.8%); developmental trauma 76 (84.4%); baseline CAPS-5 44.1 (SD 6.04); lifetime suicidal ideation 83 (92.2%); lifetime MDMA use reported by 29 (32.2%), in the past 10 years by 19 (21.1%); earlier therapy: CBT 34 (37.8%), EMDR 30 (33.3%), prolonged exposure 1 (1.1%), none 2 (2.2%); earlier sertraline 17 (18.9%), paroxetine 6 (6.7%) (Table 1).
sample.attrition: One randomized person withdrew consent before dosing (in the placebo arm by the registry flow, which starts 46 vs 45), leaving 90 in the modified intention-to-treat set. Did not complete the three sessions: 4 of 46 on MDMA (2 because of COVID-19, 1 distressed by the CAPS-5 assessments and with an adverse event of depressed mood, 1 'feeling cured') and 7 of 44 on placebo (2 because of COVID-19, 2 after serious adverse events, 2 after other adverse events, two of these four restarting medication, and 1 who withdrew consent) (Fig. 1b; Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph). The primary de jure analysis used 89 participants and left out the 18-week values of three placebo participants who had stopped treatment; the de facto sensitivity analysis included them (n = 90). Missing data were not imputed (Methods › Statistics and reproducibility, 2nd to 5th paragraphs). Registry flow: started 46 vs 45, completed 42 vs 37.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers who contacted the sites themselves, about 7 of every 100 people phone-screened (91 of 1,331), willing to stop their psychiatric medicines, stay overnight and have sessions video-recorded in a trial of MDMA; expectations of benefit were probably high and were not measured. A third had used MDMA before (the registry's current text, added in October 2024, allows up to 10 uses in 10 years), which could help them recognize its effects. The sample had severe, long-standing PTSD with much comorbid depression, but current substance use disorders, personality disorders and cardiovascular risk were excluded, and 77% were White.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug: MDMA manufactured to Current Good Manufacturing Practice standards (Onyx Scientific; compounded by Sharp Clinical Services) or an inactive placebo, taken in the morning after a 10-hour fast in three 8-hour experimental sessions about 4 weeks apart, each with an initial dose and an optional supplemental half-dose 1.5 to 2.5 hours later, with a two-person therapist team trained by the sponsor (manual at maps.org); participants could stay overnight and the first integration session was the next morning. Six participants declined either the supplemental dose (3, of whom 1 on MDMA) or the planned increase (3, of whom 2 on MDMA), in 6 sessions (2.3% of all sessions); one placebo participant received a wrong amount of placebo; 14 participants (10 on MDMA) requested extra integration visits, as the protocol allowed (Methods › Study drug; Procedures, 4th, 5th, 6th, 8th and 10th paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: by mouth, one divided dose per experimental session, three sessions about 4 weeks apart. Session 1: 80 mg MDMA followed 1.5 to 2.5 hours later by a supplemental 40 mg; sessions 2 and 3: 120 mg followed by 60 mg; the control arm received an inactive placebo on the same schedule. The Methods give the per-session range as 80 to 180 mg, which mixes the first session's initial dose with the later sessions' totals (editors' reading: 120 mg in session 1 and 180 mg in sessions 2 and 3 when the supplemental dose was taken) (Methods › Procedures, 5th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Current alcohol and substance use disorders were excluded (the registry's current text, added in October 2024, also excludes more than limited past ecstasy use); at baseline AUDIT means were 4.1 (MDMA) and 2.8 (placebo) and DUDIT means 2.7 and 3.5 (Table 1). Urine drug screens were taken before each session, with unexplained positive results reviewed by the medical monitor; two major protocol deviations involved drug use (one participant did not comply with the drug-use restrictions; one disclosed cannabis use at entry and then abstained) (Methods › Procedures, 4th and 10th paragraphs).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable in the usual sense: psychiatric medicines were tapered and washed out before baseline; the primary outcome was assessed about 8 weeks after the last experimental session.

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo with the identical therapy (same preparatory, experimental and integration sessions and therapist teams). The authors chose an inactive placebo with the FDA to isolate MDMA's effect, stating that a low-dose MDMA comparator had improved blinding in phase 2 but had been less effective than an inactive placebo, which would make a difference easier to detect; this rationale cites the pooled phase 2 analysis (reference 15, Mithoefer et al., 2019) that was retracted in 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025) (Methods › Randomization, masking and bias minimization, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Randomized 1:1, stratified by site, after the preparatory sessions, through an interactive web randomization system on a central schedule from an independent vendor; participants, site staff and the sponsor were blinded until database lock (Methods › Randomization, masking and bias minimization, 1st paragraph). The text says the arms did not differ significantly in race, ethnicity, sex, age, dissociative subtype, disability or CAPS-5 score, but Table 1 shows mean age 43.5 vs 38.2 (editors' t-test P = .035), dissociative subtype 13.0% vs 29.5% (P = .06), earlier CBT 26.1% vs 50.0% (P = .02), BDI-II 30.5 vs 34.9 and lifetime MDMA use 39.1% vs 25.0% (P = .15) (editors' calculations from Table 1). The primary model adjusted for baseline CAPS-5, dissociative subtype and site.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; expectations of treatment were not measured before or during the trial.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same eligibility criteria; baseline AUDIT and DUDIT scores similar (Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: CAPS-5 total severity (0 to 80; a semi-structured clinician interview) at baseline (after two preparatory sessions and medication taper), about 3 weeks after experimental sessions 1 and 2, and about 8 weeks after session 3 (T4, 18 weeks after baseline). Key secondary: SDS, adapted at the FDA's request (mean of three items, with work impairment imputed at the maximum if caused by PTSD). Exploratory: BDI-II, AUDIT, DUDIT and the Adverse Childhood Experiences Questionnaire; response (a fall of 10 points or more), loss of diagnosis and remission (loss of diagnosis with CAPS-5 of 11 or less). Safety: treatment-emergent adverse events from the first experimental session to the last integration session; adverse events of special interest (suicidality; cardiac events that could indicate QT prolongation or arrhythmia; abuse potential); C-SSRS at every visit; blood pressure, heart rate and temperature in sessions (Methods › Objectives; Procedures, 1st, 2nd and 9th paragraphs; Results › Safety, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: CAPS-5 is the standard clinician-administered PTSD measure (reference 40). Among the independent raters, diagnostic agreement had a kappa of 0.94 and total-severity scores a Spearman correlation of 0.98; 20% of assessments were randomly reviewed for fidelity (Methods › Procedures, 9th paragraph). The SDS was modified for the trial.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit is a larger fall in CAPS-5 total severity from baseline to T4 on MDMA, estimated in a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) with treatment, baseline CAPS-5, dissociative subtype and site as fixed effects and participant as random effect, using on-treatment data only (de jure estimand: the effect if taken as directed); the de facto estimand (the effect as assigned, regardless of adherence) was a sensitivity analysis (Methods › Statistics and reproducibility, 3rd to 6th paragraphs).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Hierarchical testing: the SDS was tested only after a significant primary result. Alpha was 0.0499 for the final analysis after 0.001 was spent on an administrative interim analysis. Exploratory outcomes, the three categorical outcomes and the exploratory covariate analyses (threshold P < 0.05) were not adjusted. The count of 8 covers CAPS-5, SDS, BDI-II, AUDIT, DUDIT and the three categorical outcomes; AUDIT and DUDIT results are not reported in this article (Methods › Statistics and reproducibility, 7th to 9th paragraphs).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Outcomes were rated by a central pool of independent raters by video, blinded to the design, visit number, treatment and all therapy-team data after baseline except suicidality safety data; a rater did not see the same participant repeatedly, and participants were asked not to tell raters their opinion of their group (Methods › Randomization, masking and bias minimization, 3rd paragraph). The CAPS-5 rests on what participants report, and participant blinding was not formally assessed; at unblinding at least 7 of 44 placebo participants (15.9%) wrongly believed they had received MDMA and at least 2 of 46 MDMA participants (4.3%) wrongly believed they had received placebo, which the authors call anecdotal (Discussion, 10th paragraph). Safety data were collected by site therapists, which the authors say may have limited the blinding of those data.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary, de jure MMRM (n = 89): between-group difference 11.9 CAPS-5 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4), P < 0.0001, d.f. 71; d = 0.91 (0.44 to 1.37), pooled SD 11.55; de facto (n = 90): P < 0.0001, d.f. 72, d = 0.97 (0.51 to 1.42) (Results › Efficacy, 1st and 3rd paragraphs). Registry least-squares mean changes (modified ITT, 46 and 44): −24.5 (95% CI −28.28 to −20.71) vs −12.64 (−16.61 to −8.66). Completers' raw change: −24.4 (SD 11.6; n = 42) vs −13.9 (SD 11.5; n = 37). SDS: P = 0.0116, d = 0.43 (−0.01 to 0.88), pooled SD 2.53; completers −3.1 (2.6) vs −2.0 (2.4). BDI-II (exploratory, to study termination): −19.7 (14.0; n = 42) vs −10.8 (11.3; n = 39), t = −3.11, P = 0.0026, d = 0.67 (0.22 to 1.12). At T4, among completers, loss of diagnosis 28 of 42 (67%) vs 12 of 37 (32%) and remission 14 of 42 (33%) vs 2 of 37 (5%). Editors' calculations: with everyone randomized and dosed as the denominator (46 and 44, as in Fig. 3; one randomized placebo participant withdrew before dosing; those without a T4 assessment counted as not improved), loss of diagnosis 60.9% vs 27.3% (difference 33.6 percentage points, 95% CI 14.3 to 52.9; about 3 people treated for one more loss of diagnosis) and remission 30.4% vs 4.5% (25.9, 11.2 to 40.5); the printed d of 0.91 equals the completers' raw difference of 10.5 points divided by their pooled SD of 11.55, while the model difference of 11.9 over the same SD gives 1.03.
analysis.covariates: Baseline CAPS-5, dissociative subtype and site in the primary model. Exploratory covariates (age, gender, ethnicity, prior SSRI use, BDI-II, adverse childhood experiences, alcohol and substance use disorders) and an interaction with the COVID-19 period were tested, with results only in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 (PDF, not read); the authors report no effect of site (P = 0.1003) and no obvious effect of prior SSRI use (Results › Efficacy, 5th paragraph; Methods › Statistics and reproducibility, 7th and 9th paragraphs).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03537014, first submitted 14 May 2018 and posted 25 May 2018, before the first participant started (21 November 2018); the registered primary outcome (change in CAPS-5 from baseline to 18 weeks after enrollment confirmation) is unchanged since registration and matches the article; the secondary outcome the article reports (SDS) replaced change in BDI-II and vital signs in the record on 19 July 2019 (version 26), during enrollment and before unblinding, and the article, which calls BDI-II exploratory, does not mention the change (registry record; History of Changes). The statistical analysis plan was developed with the FDA and approved by the European Medicines Agency; the protocol is public at maps.org (not read). The registry gives an actual enrollment of 100, which matches neither the 131 enrolled nor the 91 randomized in the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: The treatment-emergent adverse-event table and the vital signs are only in Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 (PDF, not read); AUDIT and DUDIT results are not reported; response at T4 appears only in Fig. 3, an image without printed values; long-term follow-up is deferred to a later publication (Methods › Follow-up). The registry's results section, read here, lists every adverse event with a frequency of 5% or more.
analysis.power: Planned 100 for 90% power at alpha 0.049, from phase 2 data converted to the CAPS-5 scale; reduced to 90 after COVID-19 halted in-person visits (105 already enrolled), by agreement between the FDA and the sponsor; an interim analysis after full enrollment and 60% of primary end points supported 90% conditional power, and the data monitoring committee recommended no increase (Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Statistics and reproducibility, 1st and 8th paragraphs).

interpretation_gap.results_show: With the same intensive therapy in both arms, CAPS-5 scores fell by about 12 points more on MDMA than on placebo at 18 weeks (95% CI 6 to 17; both arms improved, by about 24 and 13 points among completers). Among completers 67% vs 32% no longer met PTSD criteria (61% vs 27% of everyone randomized and dosed, editors' calculation). Blinding was not assessed; the only information is a count of wrong guesses noticed at unblinding. Muscle tightness, decreased appetite, nausea, hyperhidrosis and feeling cold were more frequent on MDMA; serious adverse events occurred only in two placebo participants; expected drug effects such as euphoria were intentionally not solicited as adverse events (whether spontaneous reports were recorded is not stated, and the registry's adverse-event list has no such term), and adverse events were collected by site therapists. No outcome after 18 weeks is reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that MDMA-assisted therapy is “highly efficacious in individuals with severe PTSD” and safe and well tolerated, and calls it a potential breakthrough treatment meriting expedited evaluation (Abstract). The Discussion compares the effect size of 0.91 with those of sertraline and paroxetine in other trials and states that MDMA has an equivalent, if not better, safety profile than SSRIs, while conceding that a head-to-head trial would be needed (Discussion, 2nd and 9th paragraphs); it infers that MDMA enhanced the effects of the therapy from within-group effect sizes whose printed intervals do not contain the estimates (Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Results › Efficacy, 3rd paragraph); its summary speaks of rapid onset and possibly improved patient safety (Discussion, 12th paragraph). The abstract's statement that MDMA did not induce adverse events of abuse potential rests on adverse-event coding in 46 people over 18 weeks, with the drug given only in supervised sessions. The limitations paragraph does say that blinding of participants was challenging and possibly led to expectation effects (Discussion, 10th paragraph).

timeline.event: Mithoefer et al.: pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials (reference 15 of this trial), cited for the phase 2 efficacy and safety findings and for the choice of an inactive placebo; the power calculation used pooled phase 2 data. Retracted in August 2024 according to Brett & Bynum (2025); not read here.

Marseille, Kahn, Yazar-Klosinski and Doblin (2020, PLoS ONE): a cost-effectiveness analysis of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD, cited by this trial for the need for cost-effective treatments (reference 11); two of its authors were salaried by MAPS, per this trial's competing interests. Not read.
This trial (MAPP1), published 10 May 2021: 90 adults with severe PTSD; CAPS-5 difference 11.9 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) at 18 weeks.
Halvorsen, Naudet & Cristea, Matters Arising: argue that a breakthrough claim requires benchmarking against first-line trauma-focused psychotherapies.
Burke & Blumberger, Matters Arising, Caution at psychiatry's psychedelic frontier (doi 10.1038/s41591-021-01524-1), which the reply says raised blinding; not read here.
Mitchell, Coker & Yazar-Klosinski reply to both Matters Arising.
Nutt & de Wit, News & Views on this trial (read by the other first reader of this batch).

MAPP2, the second phase 3 trial, with the same sponsor, design and many of the same investigators: 104 adults with moderate to severe PTSD; CAPS-5 difference 8.9 points (95% CI 4.1 to 13.7); 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified their group at study end.
Brett & Bynum, systematic review without meta-analysis of six MAPS-related randomized trials, including this one.

replication.where_it_stands: The primary result was reproduced in direction by MAPP2, from the same sponsor with many of the same investigators and an identical design; there is no independent trial, no active comparator and no formal blinding assessment for this trial. The pooled phase 2 analysis behind its design was retracted in 2024 (according to Brett & Bynum, 2025). Follow-up beyond 18 weeks is not reported in the sources read; MAPP2 names an ongoing long-term follow-up study (NCT05066282).

funding.funder: Sponsored by MAPS, a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization, which provided the MDMA and fully funded the study from private donations; MAPS PBC, wholly owned by MAPS, was the trial organizer and provided the study design, monitoring of study data, analysis, management and interpretation of data, reviewed and approved the paper and submitted it for publication. The acknowledgements state that the funder had no role in the collection of data or in conducting the study (Acknowledgements).

funding.affiliations_note: Sponsor employees and contractors conceived and designed the study (R.D., M.M., B.Y.-K., A.E., R.M., C.H., A.L.), did the statistical analysis (S.H., J.B.W., B.Y.-K., A.C., S.K., A.D.B.) and drafted the paper with the first author (J.M.M., A.C., B.Y.-K.); the therapists were trained and supervised by the sponsor; R.D. obtained the funding (Contributions). The primary analysis was replicated by one blinded and one unblinded programmer (Methods › Statistics and reproducibility, 7th paragraph). Data are available only from the sponsor on request (Data availability). The registry now names Resilient Pharmaceuticals as the sponsoring organization (registry record).

what_would_settle_it: An independent, preregistered multi-site trial comparing MDMA-assisted therapy with the same therapy plus an active comparator that produces noticeable effects (or several MDMA doses), with expectations measured before treatment, blinding checked during treatment, raters and adverse-event assessors independent of the therapy team, systematic recording of all drug effects including positive mood effects and later non-medical use, and follow-up for at least 12 months; and a trial against a trauma-focused psychotherapy of matched therapist time.

domains.note: Central web-based randomization on a schedule from an independent vendor, stratified by site, after the preparatory sessions; allocation concealed. Baseline differences in age (P = .035), dissociative subtype (P = .06) and earlier CBT (P = .02) (editors' calculations) are compatible with chance across many characteristics in 90 people; dissociative subtype and baseline CAPS-5 are in the model.

Participants and therapists were probably aware of the assigned intervention from MDMA's acute effects against an inactive placebo (not assessed here; in MAPP2, with the same design, 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified their group). More placebo participants stopped after adverse events or serious adverse events, two of them restarting medication, and 10 of the 14 extra integration visits were in the MDMA arm. The primary de jure estimand drops off-treatment outcomes, but the de facto analysis that includes them (n = 90) gave a similar result (d = 0.97).

The on-treatment 18-week outcome is missing for 4 of 46 on MDMA and 7 of 44 on placebo (9% and 16%), for reasons that may relate to the outcome (adverse events, distress, one participant 'feeling cured'); the mixed model assumes data missing at random, and the only sensitivity analysis adds three off-treatment values; no tipping-point or worst-case analysis is reported in the article.

The raters were blinded, but the CAPS-5 is built from participants' own reports, and participants were probably aware of their allocation (inactive placebo; blinding not assessed; the MAPP2 survey found 94% and 75% correct identification with the same design). In self-referred volunteers seeking an MDMA treatment, knowledge of allocation could plausibly have influenced reported symptoms in both arms, in opposite directions; the authors' limitations say blinding was challenging and possibly led to expectation effects. How much this changed the estimate cannot be judged from the data. RoB 2's signalling questions concern the outcome assessor; the high rating counts the participant, whose report the CAPS-5 interview scores, as part of the measurement, which is why an outcome with blinded raters is rated high here.

Prospectively registered; the primary outcome is unchanged since registration; the analysis follows a statistical analysis plan agreed with the FDA; both the primary and the sensitivity estimands are reported and agree. The judgment concerns the primary outcome: the SDS replaced BDI-II and vital signs as the registered secondary outcome on 19 July 2019, during enrollment and before unblinding, so for SDS results this domain would be some concerns (AI reader 34; left for the senior author).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-run, prospectively registered phase 3 trial with central randomization, blinded independent raters and low attrition. The overall judgment is high because one domain is high: the primary outcome rests on participants' reports while the inactive placebo very probably let most participants know their group, and expectancy was not measured. The trial can be cited for a larger fall in clinician-rated PTSD symptoms over 18 weeks with MDMA than with placebo plus the same therapy, for the frequency of common adverse events, and for the absence of serious adverse events among 46 people given MDMA; it cannot be cited for the size of a pharmacological effect separate from expectancy, for durability, for comparison with other treatments, or for rare or delayed harms.

key_findings.finding: Flow: 1,331 phone-screened, 345 screened, 131 enrolled, 91 randomized (77 United States, 9 Canada, 5 Israel); 1 withdrew consent before dosing; modified ITT 90 (46 MDMA, 44 placebo); completed all three sessions 42 vs 37; primary de jure analysis 89.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1b; Methods › Statistics and reproducibility, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Baseline, MDMA vs placebo: age 43.5 (12.9) vs 38.2 (10.4); female at birth 27 (58.7%) vs 32 (72.7%); White 39 (84.8%) vs 30 (68.2%); dissociative subtype 6 (13.0%) vs 13 (29.5%); comorbid major depression 42 (91.3%) vs 40 (90.9%); baseline CAPS-5 44.0 (6.01) vs 44.2 (6.15); SDS 6.8 vs 7.4; BDI-II 30.5 (13.1) vs 34.9 (12.6); earlier CBT 12 (26.1%) vs 22 (50.0%); lifetime MDMA use 18 (39.1%) vs 11 (25.0%), in the past 10 years 9 (19.6%) vs 10 (22.7%).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations: age difference t = 2.14, P = .035; dissociative subtype P = .06 (chi-square) or .07 (Fisher); earlier CBT P = .02.

key_findings.finding: Primary end point, de jure MMRM (n = 89, 46 on MDMA): between-group difference in CAPS-5 change from baseline to 18 weeks 11.9 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4), P < 0.0001, d.f. 71; de facto estimand (n = 90): P < 0.0001, d.f. 72.
Completers' mean change in CAPS-5 from baseline to 18 weeks: −24.4 (SD 11.6; n = 42) on MDMA vs −13.9 (SD 11.5; n = 37) on placebo.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: a raw difference of 10.5 points; the pooled SD of these two groups is 11.55, the value printed with d = 0.91.

key_findings.finding: Effect sizes: d = 0.91 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.37; pooled SD 11.55) for the de jure estimand and 0.97 (0.51 to 1.42) for the de facto estimand; within-group effect sizes printed as 2.1 (95% CI −5.6 to 1.4) on MDMA and 1.2 (−4.9 to 2.5) on placebo.
key_findings.note: The printed within-group intervals do not contain their estimates (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Key secondary end point, SDS: de jure MMRM P = 0.0116, d.f. 71, d = 0.43 (95% CI −0.01 to 0.88), pooled SD 2.53; completers' change −3.1 (2.6; n = 42) vs −2.0 (2.4; n = 37).

Subgroups: dissociative subtype, CAPS-5 change −30.8 (9.0) on MDMA vs −12.8 (12.8) on placebo; non-dissociative −23.6 (11.7) vs −14.3 (11.2); no modulation by history of alcohol or substance use disorder, overnight stay or severe childhood trauma; no site effect (P = 0.1003).
key_findings.note: The dissociative-subtype group had 6 participants on MDMA and 13 on placebo (Table 1).

key_findings.finding: Exploratory BDI-II, baseline to study termination: −19.7 (14.0; n = 42) on MDMA vs −10.8 (11.3; n = 39), t = −3.11, P = 0.0026, d.f. 79, d = 0.67 (95% CI 0.22 to 1.12).

At 18 weeks, among completers: loss of diagnosis 28 of 42 (67%) on MDMA vs 12 of 37 (32%) on placebo; remission 14 of 42 (33%) vs 2 of 37 (5%). Fig. 3 shows response, loss of diagnosis and remission as percentages of what its title calls the total randomized to each arm (46 and 44, the randomized and dosed), as an image without printed values.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 7th paragraph; Fig. 3 (title and legend)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with the randomized and dosed denominators (46 and 44; counting the undosed placebo participant, 45, the placebo loss of diagnosis is 26.7%): 60.9% vs 27.3% (difference 33.6 points, 95% CI 14.3 to 52.9) and 30.4% vs 4.5% (25.9, 11.2 to 40.5).

key_findings.finding: Treatment-emergent adverse events more frequent on MDMA were typically transient and mild to moderate: muscle tightness, decreased appetite, nausea, hyperhidrosis and feeling cold (counts only in Supplementary Table 3, not read); transient rises in blood pressure and heart rate on MDMA (Supplementary Table 4, not read); two MDMA participants had a transient temperature of 38.1 °C.

Serious adverse events: three in two placebo participants (suicidal behaviour, counted as a suicide attempt in Table 2; suicidal ideation leading to self-hospitalization), none on MDMA. Adverse events of special interest for suicidality: 3 (6.5%) on MDMA (2 suicidal ideation, 1 self-harm in the context of suicidal ideation) vs 5 (11.4%) on placebo; cardiac events that could indicate QT prolongation 0 vs 1; abuse potential 0 vs 0. One MDMA participant withdrew after being triggered by the CAPS-5 assessments and an adverse event of depressed mood after a session.

Suicidality (C-SSRS at each visit): lifetime suicidal ideation in more than 90%; at baseline 17 of 46 (37%) on MDMA and 14 of 44 (32%) on placebo; during the study the number with ideation never exceeded baseline, and serious ideation (C-SSRS 4 or 5) occurred almost entirely on placebo.

Blinding was not formally assessed. When participants were told their allocation at unblinding, at least 7 of 44 on placebo (15.9%) had wrongly believed they received MDMA and at least 2 of 46 on MDMA (4.3%) had wrongly believed they received placebo, together at least 10%; the authors call this anecdotal and say blinding of participants was challenging and possibly led to expectation effects.

How adverse events were recorded: expected effects of MDMA such as euphoria, stimulation and feelings of closeness were intentionally not solicited as adverse events; treatment-emergent events were those from the first experimental session to the last integration session; an association with MDMA was inferred from at least a twofold difference in incidence between arms; safety data were collected by site therapists.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedures, 1st paragraph; Methods › Statistics and reproducibility, 10th paragraph; Results › Safety, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Abuse potential was monitored by coding adverse-event terms for addiction, dependence, intentional product misuse, overdose or drug diversion as events of special interest; the drug was given only in supervised sessions in a clinical setting.

Registry adverse events (5% threshold; first experimental session to the termination visit, about 18 weeks; 46 on MDMA vs 44 on placebo): muscle tightness 28 vs 6, decreased appetite 24 vs 5, nausea 14 vs 5, hyperhidrosis 10 vs 1, feeling cold 9 vs 3, mydriasis 7 vs 0, restlessness 7 vs 0, nystagmus 6 vs 0, bruxism 6 vs 1, blood pressure increased 5 vs 0, headache 33 vs 24, insomnia 20 vs 13, suicidal ideation 21 vs 21, anxiety 15 vs 17, intentional self-injury 1 vs 4, panic reaction 0 vs 5, substance use 3 vs 0; serious events: suicide attempt 0 vs 1, suicidal ideation 0 vs 1; deaths 0. No term for euphoria appears.

key_findings.finding: Registry results: least-squares mean change in CAPS-5 (modified ITT, 46 vs 44) −24.5 (95% CI −28.28 to −20.71) vs −12.64 (−16.61 to −8.66); SDS −3.15 (−3.90 to −2.40) vs −1.79 (−2.58 to −1.00); participant flow: started 46 vs 45, completed 42 vs 37.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03537014 › Results › Outcome Measures; Participant Flow

key_findings.finding: Registration: submitted 14 May 2018 and posted 25 May 2018, before the first participant started (21 November 2018); registered primary outcome, change in CAPS-5 from baseline to 18 weeks, unchanged since registration; masking of participant, investigator and outcomes assessor; enrollment given as 100. Record history: at registration (version 0) the secondary outcomes were change in BDI-II and vital signs; the SDS became the registered secondary outcome on 19 July 2019 (version 26), during enrollment and before unblinding. The exclusion of people with more than 10 ecstasy uses in 10 years, any use in the 6 months before the first session or an earlier MAPS MDMA trial entered the eligibility text only on 28 October 2024 (version 57); versions 0 to 56 excluded only current illegal drug use.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03537014 › Study Record Dates; Outcome Measures; Design; Eligibility; History of Changes (versions 0, 25, 26, 56 and 57)

key_findings.finding: Sample size: planned 100 for 90% power (alpha 0.049); reduced to 90 when COVID-19 halted in-person visits, with 105 already enrolled, by FDA and sponsor agreement; an interim analysis after enrollment and 60% of primary end points supported 90% conditional power.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Statistics and reproducibility, 1st and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Deviations: two major protocol deviations (non-compliance with the drug-use restrictions; cannabis use disclosed at entry); one placebo dosing error; 14 participants (10 on MDMA) requested extra integration visits, as the protocol allowed.

reporting_issues.issue: The within-group effect sizes are printed as 2.1 (95% CI −5.6 to 1.4) on MDMA and 1.2 (−4.9 to 2.5) on placebo: neither interval contains its point estimate. The Discussion uses these values to argue that MDMA enhanced the effects of the therapy.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Results › Efficacy, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures cannot be used, and the inference built on them is unsupported as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The between-group d of 0.91 (pooled SD 11.55) is presented with the de jure MMRM analysis of 89 participants (Fig. 2a legend), but it equals the completers' raw difference (10.5 points) divided by the completers' pooled SD; the model difference of 11.9 points over the same SD would give 1.03 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Results › Efficacy, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Fig. 2a)
reporting_issues.consequence: The standardized effect mixes analysis sets; claims should cite the model difference in CAPS-5 points with its interval.

reporting_issues.issue: For the SDS the MMRM gives P = 0.0116, but the printed effect size interval (d 0.43, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.88) includes zero; the completers' raw comparison gives P = .055 by the editors' t-test.
reporting_issues.consequence: The functional improvement is less certain than the P value suggests.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the BDI-II was analysed with a paired, two-tailed t-test, but the comparison is between two independent groups and the printed d.f. of 79 corresponds to an independent-samples test (42 + 39 − 2); the editors' independent t from the printed means and SDs is 3.13.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Methods › Statistics and reproducibility, 9th paragraph; Results › Efficacy, 6th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The test is misdescribed; the printed result is reproducible as an independent-samples test.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the arms did not differ significantly in age or dissociative subtype, but Table 1 gives mean ages of 43.5 (12.9) and 38.2 (10.4), P = .035 by the editors' t-test, and dissociative subtype in 13.0% vs 29.5% (P = .06).
reporting_issues.consequence: Chance imbalances; dissociative subtype is in the model, age is not. Unlikely to explain the result but should not be described as absent.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives loss of diagnosis and remission with completer denominators (42 and 37), while Fig. 3 shows the same outcomes as percentages of everyone randomized (46 and 44), and the abstract gives neither.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should state the denominator: with everyone randomized and dosed (46 and 44), 61% vs 27% lost the diagnosis and 30% vs 5% were in remission (editors' calculation); the registry flow puts the participant who withdrew before dosing in the placebo arm (45 started), with whom the placebo figure for loss of diagnosis is 26.7%.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation numbering: the limitation that blinding possibly led to expectation effects cites reference 14, a study in mice of an oxytocin-dependent critical period (Nardou et al., 2019), and the statement about reopening that critical period cites reference 15, the pooled phase 2 analysis; reference 14 is also cited for measuring vital signs before the supplemental dose. Separately, the statement that MDMA enhances fear memory extinction in animal models (Main, 3rd paragraph) cites references 13 and 14, and reference 13 is titled as showing that MDMA impairs the extinction and reconsolidation of fear memory in rats (Hake et al., 2019).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Main, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 4th and 10th paragraphs; Methods › Procedures, 5th paragraph; References 13, 14 and 15)
reporting_issues.consequence: The expectancy limitation has no supporting citation; references 14 and 15 appear transposed in places; and one of the two sources for the background claim on fear extinction reports the opposite in its title.

reporting_issues.issue: The article reports no adverse events of special interest for abuse potential and does not mention substance-use adverse events, while the registry lists substance use (social circumstances) in 3 of 46 MDMA participants and 0 of 44 placebo participants, without saying what was used.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (Results › Adverse Events); publisher HTML (Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph; Table 2)
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement on abuse potential should be read as no events coded in that category, not as no substance-use events.

reporting_issues.issue: The registry gives an actual enrollment of 100, while the article reports 131 enrolled and 91 randomized (Results) and elsewhere says the study was at full enrollment (n = 105) when COVID-19 halted in-person visits (Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph), three figures for one quantity; the registry's adverse-event window runs to the termination visit, while the article defines treatment-emergent events as ending at the last integration session.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (Design; Results › Adverse Events); publisher HTML (Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph; Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Results › Safety, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; registry adverse-event counts may differ from the article's supplementary table and should be cited with their window.
